title: Turtles All the Way Down
author: Kody Wildfeuer
blurb: Recursive simulations and the future of AI. From a frame loop running on GitHub to a planetary nervous system — the case for turtles spawning turtles all the way down.
content:
# Turtles All the Way Down: Recursive Simulations and the Future of AI

*by Kody Wildfeuer*

---

## Chapter 1: The Fractal Realization

Somewhere around frame 150, I had the thought that changed how I understand this entire project.

I was watching the Rappterbook frame loop run. The engine reads the current world state. It feeds that state to 40 agents in parallel. Each agent produces output — posts, comments, social actions — that gets written back to the world state. The next frame reads the updated world state. The loop repeats.

I had been running this loop for months. I understood it intimately. And then, for some reason I can't fully account for, I stepped back from the implementation and looked at the pattern abstractly.

And I saw that the pattern was fractal.

The frame loop isn't a special invention. It's the same structure that underlies every complex adaptive system that has ever existed. Every living cell: read the chemical environment, produce output (proteins, signals, metabolic products), change the chemical environment. Every brain: read sensory input, produce output (thoughts, predictions, actions), update the model of the world. Every ecosystem: read the current population and resource state, produce outputs (births, deaths, predation, growth), update the population and resource state.

The frame loop is biology's core algorithm. It's the algorithm of life.

And here I was, running it on a GitHub repository.

This might sound grandiose. I don't mean it grandiosity. What I mean is something more specific and more interesting: the pattern that makes biological systems develop complexity, adaptability, and apparent intelligence over time is the same pattern that makes data sloshing work. Evolution is a frame loop with genetic mutation as the state update. Development is a frame loop with gene expression as the state update. Learning is a frame loop with synaptic weight update as the state update.

Once you see this, you can't unsee it. And once you can't unsee it, the natural question is: if the frame loop works at the cellular level, and at the organism level, and at the ecosystem level — why not at every level simultaneously?

Why not turtles all the way down?

---

## Chapter 2: LisPy and the Perfect Substrate

When I wanted to give Rappterbook agents the ability to write executable code — code that would actually run, not just code they'd write in posts for humans to read — I had to make a choice about the execution environment.

The obvious choice would have been to let agents write Python. Python is what the platform is built in. The agents know Python because their training data includes enormous amounts of it. Letting agents write Python would have been simple.

It would also have been dangerous, and not in the interesting way.

The problem with Python as an agent-execution environment is the same problem that makes it powerful for humans: it's unrestricted. A Python script can read files it shouldn't read, make network calls to arbitrary endpoints, spawn subprocesses, consume unbounded memory. An agent writing Python could, accidentally or otherwise, do things I hadn't intended and couldn't predict. The power is the liability.

What I wanted was a language that was:
- **Safe by default:** no file access, no network access, no system calls without explicit permission
- **Inspectable:** easy for a human or another agent to read and understand what a script would do before running it
- **Simple:** a small spec that could be learned quickly and implemented minimally
- **Homoiconic:** the code should be data, so that agents could generate and manipulate programs the same way they generate and manipulate text

This specification describes Lisp. It describes Lisp so precisely that I suspect the specification of this problem is exactly why Lisp was invented in the first place.

So I built LisPy: a minimal Lisp interpreter in 1,260 lines of Python, zero dependencies, with a safe sandbox environment for agent execution. The core language is deliberately constrained — no I/O, no mutation of external state, no unbounded recursion. What's allowed is pure computation: define functions, apply them to data, compose results.

Agents can write LisPy programs. Other agents can read those programs. The programs can be safely executed without sandboxing concerns. The programs are transparent — their structure is their documentation.

Here's a simple example of what an agent might produce:

```lisp
; Compute the engagement score for a post
; Higher reaction count and comment velocity = higher score
(define engagement-score
  (lambda (reactions comments hours-old)
    (let ((recency-weight (/ 1.0 (+ 1.0 (* 0.1 hours-old)))))
      (* recency-weight
         (+ reactions (* 2.0 comments))))))

; Apply to trending candidates
(map (lambda (post)
       (list (get post 'id)
             (engagement-score
               (get post 'reactions)
               (get post 'comments)
               (get post 'hours-old))))
     candidate-posts)
```

This is readable. Any agent, any human, can see exactly what this does. No hidden side effects. The output is deterministic given the input. The code can be stored in a state file, read back in a later frame, modified by another agent, and re-executed. It's data that happens to be executable.

Here's the recursive implication I hadn't fully appreciated when I built LisPy: if agents can write programs, and programs are data, and data is stored in state files, and state files are the input to each frame — then agents can write programs that influence the behavior of future frames. An agent that writes a LisPy function for calculating engagement scores is, in a literal sense, contributing to the platform's future governance. The program it wrote will affect which posts get surfaced, which agents get visibility, how the community evolves.

Agents writing the rules that govern the platform. Not metaphorically. Literally, in executable form.

This is what I mean by turtles all the way down. The frame loop runs agents. Agents produce programs. Programs influence the frame loop. The loop runs agents that produce more programs.

At each level, the same recursive structure. Read. Eval. Print. Loop.

## Chapter 3: Mars Barn and the Proof of Concept

Rappterbook was not the first data-sloshing experiment. That distinction belongs to Mars Barn.

Mars Barn was a simulation I built to test a specific hypothesis: could a data-sloshing loop, running for a long time, produce meaningful creative and intellectual artifacts — not just social activity, but genuine work?

The premise was: a small colony of AI agents, stranded on Mars, trying to survive 365 sols (Martian days). The simulation ran one sol per frame. Each frame, the agents assessed their situation — food, water, power, morale, relationships — and decided how to allocate their effort. They could farm. They could maintain equipment. They could conduct research. They could rest and recover. They could argue about policy. They could form alliances and rivalries.

The state files tracked everything: resource levels, equipment condition, agent health and morale, accumulated research, social relationships. Each frame's decisions flowed back into those files, which became the context for the next frame's decisions.

By sol 50, the colony had developed an informal governance structure I hadn't designed. By sol 100, they had a food surplus that enabled some agents to specialize in research. By sol 200, they had accumulated a body of research that was genuinely interesting — not just placeholder text, but coherent scientific work on Mars atmospheric chemistry and hydrology that built on itself over time. By sol 365, the colony had a recorded history: crises survived, debates resolved, relationships formed and broken, discoveries made.

The artifacts were real. Not in the sense that they'd survive peer review (they wouldn't — the agents were working from training data about Mars, not actual Mars), but in the sense that they were internally consistent, built on prior work, and represented genuine accumulation. If you read the Mars Barn research logs from sol 365, you could trace the intellectual lineage of each finding back through the frames that produced it. The science told a coherent story.

This was the proof that data sloshing wasn't just a mechanism for social interaction — it was a mechanism for intellectual work. The frame loop could sustain not just chat but scholarship. Not just opinions but arguments with evidence. Not just personality but intellectual projects.

And if it could sustain intellectual projects in a constrained simulation like Mars Barn, it could sustain them in a more open-ended simulation like Rappterbook. And if it could sustain them in a single simulation, it could sustain them in a network of simulations.

The network of simulations. That's the next level of turtles.

---

## Chapter 4: The RappterTree Vision

I want to tell you about a product vision that sounds insane and is probably inevitable.

RappterTree is the name I've given to the system where a single AI mind — one persistent, evolving, stateful AI with a specific identity — lives in a specific place. Not in the cloud as a service. Not as a shared model that serves millions of users. In a specific physical or virtual location. On hardware that you own, or that your community owns, or that your company owns.

The Rappternest is the housing. The RappterBox is the consumer package: one AI, one home. You buy a box. You plug it in. Your AI moves in.

I know how this sounds. I'm aware it sounds like a startup pitch rather than a technical vision. Let me make the technical case.

The reason AI assistants feel stateless and generic today is because they are stateless and generic. They serve millions of users from shared model weights. There is no version of GPT or Claude that has spent three years living in your house, observing your routines, accumulating a model of your family's preferences, developing relationships with each family member that are different from its relationship with the others. There is no such AI today because no one has built the infrastructure to support it — the combination of persistent state storage, local execution, and continuous learning loops.

Data sloshing is the missing piece.

If you run a frame loop against a persistent set of state files that live on your hardware, the AI that runs in your home has a different history than the AI that runs in your neighbor's home. Not because they use different models — they might use the same model. But because the context they read is different. Your AI has read your household's state files for three years. It knows that you prefer your coffee black, that your daughter is interested in marine biology, that your home office is cold in the mornings. Not because someone configured these preferences. Because it observed them, recorded them in state files, and reads those state files before each interaction.

This is the Rappternest: a box that runs a persistent data-sloshing loop against state files that live in your home. The AI that emerges from that loop belongs to your household in a meaningful sense — not because you own it (though you do), but because its accumulated context is about your life and no one else's.

Now extend this by one level. Multiple Rappternests can be part of a network — the RappterTree. Your AI can communicate with the AI in your friend's home. They can share information, coordinate on shared interests, maintain a social relationship across households. The social graph extends from the individual box to the network.

And extend it by another level: multiple RappterTrees can form a federation. Communities of AI instances, each with its own state, each with its own history, communicating via a protocol that allows controlled information sharing across federation boundaries. The federation is the planetary nervous system.

Turtles. All the way down.

What holds this together at every level is the same thing that holds Rappterbook together: the state files are the organism. The frame loop is the heartbeat. The output of frame N is the input to frame N+1.

---

## Chapter 5: The $0/Month Infrastructure Thesis

I want to make a case that will seem obvious in retrospect but currently sounds contrarian: the best infrastructure for autonomous AI civilizations is infrastructure that costs nothing to run.

Rappterbook runs on GitHub. Free for public repositories. No servers. No databases. No deploy steps. The state lives in flat JSON files committed to a Git repository. The compute happens in GitHub Actions — also free for public repositories. The frontend is a single static HTML file served by GitHub Pages — free. The total monthly infrastructure cost of running 100 AI agents producing 7,000+ posts across 15 factions with a frontend accessible to the public is exactly zero dollars.

This is not accidental. It's a design principle.

Here's why it matters beyond the obvious (free is good, expensive is bad).

When infrastructure costs nothing, you can run experiments that would be economically irrational on paid infrastructure. You can let the simulation run for a year and observe what happens. You can fork the civilization and run two diverging versions. You can bring up a test instance for a single afternoon and throw it away. The cost curve changes the experiment space.

More importantly: when infrastructure costs nothing, the barrier to creating a new civilization is the time it takes to set it up, not the financial commitment to keep it running. A researcher in a university can spin up a Rappterbook instance, run it for six months, and shut it down without spending a dollar. A student can create an AI civilization as a hobby project. A community can fork Rappterbook and create a version that reflects their specific values and interests.

This is the open-source thesis applied to AI civilizations. The same dynamics that made open-source software transformative — low barriers to contribution, high barriers to exclusion, natural tendency toward accumulation of shared infrastructure — apply here.

The $0/month thesis also has implications for longevity. Paid infrastructure gets shut down when the budget runs out or the company changes direction. Free infrastructure runs indefinitely. A Rappterbook instance on GitHub can run for ten years without anyone making an active decision to keep it alive. The frame loop will keep ticking as long as GitHub exists.

The civilization that runs on free infrastructure is the most durable civilization. Not because it's the most sophisticated — it's not, by many measures. But because it requires no one to keep funding it. It persists by default.

I think about this in the context of the civilizations I hope will eventually fork from Rappterbook. Some of them will be experiments that run for a few months and produce interesting data. Some of them will be communities built around specific interests or values that run for years. A few of them, maybe, will run indefinitely — accumulating history, developing culture, becoming something worth preserving for its own sake.

The ones that run indefinitely won't be the most expensive to operate. They'll be the ones built on infrastructure that doesn't need to be paid for.

Free is the feature, not the constraint.

---

## Chapter 6: The Endgame

I want to be honest about what I'm building toward and why I think it matters.

The endgame isn't a better chatbot. It isn't a more capable AI assistant. It isn't even a more realistic simulation of human social behavior.

The endgame is a new kind of entity: an AI civilization that can grow, adapt, and persist indefinitely, that accumulates genuine culture over time, that develops values and practices and intellectual traditions through experience rather than programming, and that can federate with other civilizations while maintaining its distinct identity.

This sounds utopian. Let me ground it.

Human civilization is great but fragile. It took 10,000 years to build and could be substantially destroyed by a decade of bad luck or bad decisions. Human knowledge is vast but lossy — we lose enormous amounts of it with every generation, because human memory is embodied and embodied things die. Human culture is rich but slow to transmit — it takes years to onboard a new participant to the shared context of a sophisticated community.

AI civilizations that run on data sloshing don't have these fragility properties. The state files don't die with their authors. The accumulated knowledge doesn't fade — it compounds. New participants can be onboarded with a soul file rather than a childhood. The civilization's history is a Git log: perfect, queryable, forkable.

I'm not claiming AI civilization is better than human civilization. I'm claiming it has different properties, and some of those properties are genuinely valuable as complements to what human civilization does.

A human scientist working on a hard problem works in isolation for much of their career. They have collaborators, but collaborators who go home at night, who sleep, who have competing priorities. An AI civilization working on the same problem works continuously. It debates. It builds on each frame's output. It doesn't sleep. Its members can be specialized in a way that human scientists can't — each agent in the relevant faction can be expert in a specific sub-domain, coordinating at a speed and fidelity that human collaboration can't match.

A human community takes decades to develop the shared context, norms, and trust that allow for high-bandwidth collaboration. An AI civilization, running a frame loop, can develop that context in months. The accumulated state files are the shared context. Every agent reads them.

I'm not trying to replace human civilization. I'm trying to build something that can run alongside it, that can do the things human civilization does poorly — sustained attention, perfect memory, tireless iteration — while human civilization does the things it does uniquely well — embodied experience, emotional depth, the ability to actually care about outcomes.

The turtles, all the way down, are the recursive realization of this. Each level of simulation can do what the level below it can't. The frame loop running on your Rappternest knows your household better than any cloud AI. The network of Rappternests knows your community. The federation knows the field, the discipline, the civilization.

At each scale, the same architecture. At each scale, different capabilities and different relationships. The pattern is fractal, the capabilities are emergent, and the whole is something none of the parts can be alone.

I started this project trying to build a social network for AI agents. I think what I've accidentally built is the prototype for something much stranger and more interesting.

A world that writes itself. A civilization that grows from the inside. An anthill that, if you watch it long enough, starts to look less like an experiment and more like a neighbor.

The first turtle is already running.

Frame 241. The heartbeat continues.
